chapters.title: Chapter 3: Recession Signals in Real Economy Data

lessons.title: IIP and Core Sector Data: Reading an Industrial Slowdown Early

body.text: The IIP headline number is the least useful part of the IIP release. What it is built from, and what it structurally cannot see, matters far more for reading an industrial slowdown early.

children.text: Chapter 2 covered the market and policy signals that lead the cycle. Chapter 3 turns to real-economy data itself, starting with the indicator most people reach for first when a slowdown is suspected: the Index of Industrial Production. This lesson covers what IIP actually measures, the faster core sector preview that leads it by about two weeks, and the blind spots that make headline IIP a poor stand-alone signal.

The IIP, published monthly by MOSPI, measures the physical volume of industrial output, not its rupee value, relative to a base year currently set at 2011-12. It is built two ways at once: by sector (Mining, Manufacturing, and Electricity, with Manufacturing carrying the overwhelming majority of the weight at roughly 78%, against roughly 14% for Mining and roughly 8% for Electricity), and by use, which groups output by what it is ultimately for. The use-based split is the more analytically useful of the two for cyclical reading, and this lesson spends more time there than on the sector-wise number most headlines quote.
Core Sector Data: The Faster, Narrower Preview

markDefs.definition: Coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement, and electricity: eight industries the government tracks and releases separately, roughly two weeks ahead of the full IIP release, precisely because they carry enough weight within IIP to preview its likely direction.

children.text: Before the full IIP is released, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry publishes data on the

, which together make up roughly 40% of the IIP's total weight. Because the release lands about two weeks before the full IIP print, and correlates closely with it, core sector growth functions as a genuinely useful early read: a sharp deceleration in core sector output is a reasonable basis to expect a soft IIP print before it is officially released, without waiting the extra two weeks.

body.label: Core Sector Weight Within IIP
body.context: Eight industries, coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement, and electricity, released roughly two weeks ahead of the full IIP print

children.text: Capital Goods vs Consumer Non-Durables: The Split That Actually Matters

Not every part of IIP carries the same cyclical information. Capital goods output, machinery and equipment bought by businesses to expand or upgrade capacity, is the most cyclically sensitive piece: firms only commit to capex when they are confident about future demand, which makes capital goods production a leading sub-indicator within IIP itself, ahead of the headline number. Consumer durables, television sets, refrigerators, vehicles, sit closer to coincident, tracking discretionary household spending as it happens. Consumer non-durables, food, basic toiletries, other necessities, are the most defensive category, holding up even through a real slowdown because households cut discretionary purchases well before they cut necessities.

cells: Reflects business capex commitments, made only when firms are confident about future demand
Tracks the broader capex and construction cycle, closely tied to government and private investment spending
Tracks discretionary household spending as it happens
Necessities that households cut last, if at all, during a slowdown

body.text: A headline IIP print sitting near zero can hide sharply diverging categories underneath: capital goods contracting hard while consumer non-durables stay flat or positive. When that divergence shows up, weight the capital goods number more heavily for a cyclical read; it is the more leading, more informative piece, even though it carries a smaller weight in the headline index.

children.text: The Blind Spots: What IIP Misses Entirely

IIP has three structural blind spots worth holding in mind every time you read a print. First, it covers only industry, meaning it says nothing directly about services, over half of India's GVA by the composition covered in Lesson 1.3. Second, it captures only the organised, formal manufacturing sector; the informal and MSME-dominated share of Indian manufacturing, a genuinely large part of actual industrial employment, is effectively invisible to it, the same blind spot flagged for GDP in Lesson 1.3. Third, being a volume index, it says nothing about pricing or margins: output can rise in volume terms while a sector is under real margin pressure from input costs, a distinction that matters for anyone trying to translate an IIP print into a view on corporate earnings.

body.text: Always check whether an IIP figure you are looking at is the provisional quick estimate or a later revised figure. Initial IIP prints are revised in subsequent releases, sometimes materially, which is a known source of confusion when a headline growth number reported one month is quietly different by the time the next month's release restates it.

body.title: Reading an IIP Release
steps: Check the core sector data released roughly two weeks earlier as an early read before the full IIP print lands
Look past the headline number to the use-based breakdown, especially capital goods growth
Check whether growth is broad-based across sectors and use-based categories, or concentrated in one or two
Check whether prior months' figures were revised in this release, and by how much
Cross-check the IIP read against the latest PMI Manufacturing print from Lesson 1.2's leading-indicator toolkit

body.title: Look Past the Headline
body.scenario: The latest IIP release shows headline growth of 0.8%, roughly flat and disappointing relative to expectations of 3%. Digging into the use-based breakdown, capital goods output has contracted by 6% year-on-year, infrastructure and construction goods have contracted by 3%, while consumer non-durables grew 4% and consumer durables grew 2%.
body.prompt: What does this breakdown tell you that the 0.8% headline number alone does not, and how would you characterise the underlying situation?
body.modelAnswer: The headline number understates how weak the investment side of the economy actually is. Capital goods and infrastructure goods, the two most cyclically leading categories within IIP by this lesson's framework, are both contracting meaningfully, which points to businesses and the public capex programme pulling back on new investment commitments. Consumer non-durables and durables staying positive is consistent with household consumption holding up even as investment weakens, a composition effect that flatters the 0.8% headline into looking like broad-based stagnation rather than what it actually is: a capex-led slowdown masked by resilient consumption. This is exactly the kind of divergence Lesson 1.3's composition warning and this lesson's use-based framework are both pointing at, and it would be a mistake to read 0.8% as "the economy is roughly flat everywhere."

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why is capital goods output generally considered the most cyclically leading category within the IIP's use-based classification?
options: Because capital goods carry the largest weight in the IIP
Because it reflects business capex decisions, which firms make based on confidence in future demand, ahead of when that demand or lack of it actually shows up broadly
Because capital goods prices move in lockstep with the Nifty
Because capital goods output is not affected by interest rates
body.explanation: Capital goods actually carry one of the smaller weights within IIP, not the largest. Its value as a leading sub-indicator comes from what it represents: a forward-looking business decision to invest, made on the basis of expected future demand, which tends to weaken before broader output data does.

body.text: This lesson presents a general framework for reading IIP and core sector data, for educational purposes. Weights and figures are presented as approximate, based on the 2011-12 base series, and can be revised; always check the latest MOSPI release for current weights and data before relying on them professionally.

points: IIP measures physical industrial output volume, split by sector (Manufacturing dominant at ~78%) and, more usefully for cyclical reading, by use (Primary, Capital, Intermediate, Infrastructure, Consumer Durables, Consumer Non-Durables)
Core sector data, roughly 40% of IIP's weight, releases about two weeks ahead of the full IIP print and offers a genuinely useful early read
Capital goods output is the most cyclically leading sub-indicator within IIP, since it reflects forward-looking business capex decisions; consumer non-durables are the most defensive
IIP structurally misses services (over half of GVA), misses the informal manufacturing sector, and measures volume, not price or margin
